title: Health centers: the federal report, the State filing and the City ledger
question: Does a health center tell the federal government and the State the same story about its patients and costs, and does the local money it reports match what the City paid?
finding: 7 San Francisco health centers file yearly counts with the federal health-center program; for 2 of them the federal figures sit badly with the State filing, the Bay Area norm or the City ledger. Strongest: San Francisco Community Health Center (reports as Asian and Pacific Islander Wellness Center): cost per patient in 2025 was $6,137, 1.7 times the median of the 10 Bay Area centers whose cost is published; reported cost went from $5.4 million in 2023 to $16.6 million in 2024 while patients went from 1,938 to 2,720; it reported $3.8 million in local-government grants for 2025, and the City ledger shows about $10.9 million paid to it that year.
how: Total patients, total cost and local-government grants from each center's federal Uniform Data System report were set beside the patients the same operator reported to the State for its licensed San Francisco clinics, the Bay Area median cost per patient among centers whose cost is published that year, and City payments for the same calendar year (the average of the two fiscal years it spans).
limits: These records are not built the same way. The federal report covers only the sites and services inside the federally approved project, which can be a small part of a large organization, so fewer patients in the federal report than in the State filing is not flagged. The State figures used here are for licensed clinics in San Francisco only, counted clinic by clinic, so a patient seen at two clinics is counted twice and a center with clinics in other counties reports more federally. A center's first federal report can cover part of a year, and a center can widen its approved project, which moves existing costs into the report. Federal money that reaches a center through the City (HIV care funds, for example) is reported as federal, not local, and City payments for work outside the health center are not in the federal report at all. The federal public file leaves many cost and visit cells blank, so the Bay Area median rests on a handful of centers. No tax-return patient count was found for these centers, so that third count is missing. A gap is a question for the organization, not proof of an error. The fiscal year of a City payment here is the Controller's: the year its files put the payment under, the same year the organization pages show. For a small part of the money the voucher was issued in an earlier fiscal year than that: $97.3 million of the $10.22 billion in the City's nonprofit spending file for the nonprofits profiled here, going by the matching lines of the payment file; for a further $152.7 million the payment file has no matching lines, or lines that mix payments and reversals, so it cannot be said.
